cards.title: Private randomness in algorithmic secret-key agreement
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Historical question, answered by the 2020 follow-up and its expanded 2024 version: does the worst-case communication barrier min{C(x|y),C(y|x)}−O(log n) for secret-key agreement persist when Alice and Bob use independent private random bits? The answer is affirmative for the bounded-error secret-key task below. In particular, on a hard family of pairs of n-bit inputs with C(x|y), C(y|x) and I(x:y) all equal to n/2 within O(log n), every uniformly computable protocol that succeeds on the promised inputs with probability greater than 1/2 has worst-case communication at least n/2−O(log n). This holds even for a secret key of length δ(n)=ω(log n), instead of the maximal length I(x:y)−O(log n). The follow-up explicitly identifies this as its answer to the source’s Open Question 1.
cards.why: Establishes that hidden local randomness cannot remove the worst-case communication needed to turn algorithmic correlation into a shared secret. This isolates communication as a resource distinct from computational hardness and from the amount of mutual information.

cards.definitions: Fix an optimal plain universal description machine U and a computable encoding of tuples. C(x|y) is the minimum bit length of a program p with U(p,y)=x; C(x)=C(x|empty string), C(x,y)=C(⟨x,y⟩), and I(x:y)=C(x)+C(y)−C(x,y). Alice receives x∈{0,1}ⁿ and Bob receives y∈{0,1}ⁿ. Both additionally receive the exact complexity profile p=(C(x),C(y),C(x,y)); the profile and the fixed protocol are public. This small auxiliary input is supplied, not computed from x or y. The parties use independent fair private coin sequences, independent of the fixed input pair. They exchange messages on a public noiseless channel, then separately output strings z_A,z_B. The transcript t records all publicly communicated bits and their order; actual transmitted framing is charged too. Cost is the worst-case total number of communicated bits over legal inputs and coin outcomes, not its expectation. The same finite algorithms compute messages and outputs for all n. Local computation and the number of interaction rounds have no polynomial bound; the protocol must terminate on every input and coin outcome, even for invalid auxiliary profiles, where output correctness is not required. The expanded result permits any finite number of private random bits, without a polynomial bound in n. Success means z_A=z_B=z of the requested length and C(z|t,p)≥|z|−O(log n), so agreement on a public string does not qualify as secrecy. Probability is over the private coins, separately for each promised input pair; x,y need not come from an independent, identically distributed or computable source. The hard-family profile equalities and lower bound mean additive deviations bounded by fixed multiples of log₂(n+2) for sufficiently large n; these constants can depend on U and the fixed protocol, not on n or its coin outcomes. The notation δ(n)=ω(log n) means δ(n)/log₂(n+2)→∞. Only attainable secret-key lengths are relevant; the maximal length is I(x:y) up to logarithmic terms.
cards.answer_criterion: The historical communication-barrier question is settled for bounded-error secret-key agreement by the follow-up’s Theorem 2, together with the earlier matching upper bound. The recorded quantitative theorem has success probability greater than 1/2 and incompressible secret keys. The original Theorem 7 was phrased more generally using arbitrary positive constant success probability and a lower bound directly on conditional key complexity; this review does not claim that the follow-up’s displayed theorem reproduces every such parameter verbatim. It records the follow-up’s explicit resolution of the usual secret-key task and its precise scope.
